name: Noor Haddad
headline: ML platform engineer. I make training and serving boring so researchers don't have to think about it.
summary: Eight years building the plumbing under machine learning teams: GPU scheduling, feature pipelines, model serving and the evals that tell you a release is safe. Last role was tech lead for ML infrastructure at a 300-person health-tech company. I want a small platform team at a company where the models matter to someone's day.

deal_breakers: No defence, gambling or ad targeting work.
No primary on-call more often than one week in six.
Not looking to manage people full-time yet; tech lead is fine.
nice_to_haves: A research team that ships to real users
Budget for conferences and open source time
Four-day week, or a clear path to it
open_to.notes: Staff ML platform or infra lead roles at companies where the models matter: health, climate, science. Remote in Europe or hybrid in Berlin.
Happy to advise early ML teams on platform and evals.

projects.title: Fair-share GPU scheduler
projects.summary: Replaced a shared Slack channel of 'who is using the A100s' with a Kubernetes scheduler extension that queues training jobs by team quota and preempts politely.
projects.outcome: GPU utilisation went from 41% to 78%; median wait for a training slot fell from 9 hours to 40 minutes.

projects.title: Release gate for clinical LLM features
projects.role: Designed and built it, then handed it to the applied team
projects.summary: Every model or prompt change runs 1,900 graded cases (clinician-written) before it can ship. Failing cases block the deploy and open a ticket with a diff of the outputs.
projects.outcome: Caught 14 regressions in six months that would have reached patients' summaries; the clinicians now write the tests themselves.

projects.title: Model serving on one platform
projects.summary: Moved 23 models from hand-rolled Flask services onto one serving layer with canaries, shadow traffic and per-model dashboards.
projects.outcome: Deploys went from a two-day ticket to a merge; p95 latency down 35%; one on-call rota instead of five.

projects.title: Streaming feature store
projects.summary: Online and offline features from the same definitions, fed by Kafka, so training and serving stop disagreeing.
projects.outcome: Removed a whole class of training/serving skew bugs; 31 features in production by year end.

projects.title: Support triage assistant
projects.role: Prototype in a two-week hack, then productionised with one other engineer
projects.summary: Retrieval over 40k past tickets suggests a category, a reply draft and the three most similar resolved cases.
projects.outcome: First-response time down 28%; agents accept the suggested category 83% of the time.

projects.title: Open source: pipeline step caching plugin
projects.summary: A small plugin for an open-source ML pipeline framework that caches step outputs by content hash across runs and machines.
projects.outcome: About 1,100 GitHub stars; merged upstream in 2024. The docs are the part people thank me for.

experience.title: Tech lead, ML infrastructure
experience.summary: Built and led the ML platform team (3 → 5). Owned training infra, serving and the eval gate.

experience.title: Senior data engineer
experience.summary: Streaming pipelines and the first feature store; moved the team from cron to an orchestrator.

experience.title: Research engineer
experience.summary: Kept a 40-GPU lab cluster alive; co-author on two papers about scheduling.

faq.a: The platform is in good shape and the team is self-sufficient; I'd like to build the next one from an earlier stage. No drama, and they're a reference.
Not as a full-time manager yet. I like being tech lead for 3-6 engineers: setting direction, reviewing designs, running hiring loops, mentoring. I'd talk about management in a year or two.
Five years on rotation, including a year as incident commander for the ML platform. I'm fine with on-call that's shared fairly and with good runbooks. One week in six is my limit for primary.

faq.q: Have you run Kafka in production?
faq.a: Yes, for three years at Freightline and Kliniq: the feature store's online path, around 20k events a second at peak. I'm comfortable operating it but I'm not a Kafka internals person.

faq.q: How much LLM work have you done?
faq.a: Two years: the eval gate for clinical summaries and the support triage assistant. My strength is the infrastructure and evaluation around models, not training foundation models.
Remote within Europe, or hybrid in Berlin or Amsterdam up to three days a week. I'm not relocating in 2027.
No, I'm an EU citizen. I can't work for a US entity directly without an employer of record.

faq.q: What does a great first 90 days look like?
faq.a: Week one: ship something small. First month: shadow on-call, interview every researcher about where their time goes. By day 90: one painful thing measurably gone and a written six-month platform plan the team agrees with.
I'm between roles, so I can start on 1 January 2027 or a little earlier for the right team.

faq.q: What kind of team do you work best in?
faq.a: Small, written-first, with researchers close by. I like design docs, honest postmortems and teams that delete code.

references.quote: Noor turned our GPU budget from our biggest argument into a solved problem, and wrote it down so well that nobody needs her to run it.

references.name: Tomás Ruiz

references.quote: She made shipping safe without making it slow. Clinicians trust our releases now.
